title: English Usually Needs a Subject
html:
Chapter 1

English Usually Needs a Subject

Sentence Foundations
Big Idea

English usually needs a visible subject.

Simple Rule

English sentence pattern: subject + verb.

Spanish Comparison

Spanish often allows the subject to disappear because the verb ending gives enough information.

Contrast box

Spanish thinkingNatural English
Hablo inglés.I speak English.
Common Mistake
IncorrectCorrect
Speak English.I speak English.
Why This Happens

This mistake makes sense. Spanish and English organize this idea differently. The goal is not to think “Spanish is wrong,” but to notice where Spanish patterns can interfere with English sentence-building. Once you see the pattern, you can practice the English structure as a whole phrase.

Real English Examples
  • I work every day.
  • She lives in Florida.
  • They study English.
  • It is raining.
  • We have class today.
  • You speak Spanish.
  • He needs help.
  • The teacher explains the lesson.
Practice
  1. Fix the mistake: Speak English.
  2. Translate into English: Hablo inglés
  3. Build your own sentence using the rule from this chapter.
  4. Choose the correct answer: I speak English. / Speak English.
Show answers
  1. I speak English.
  2. Answers may vary, but they should follow the chapter pattern.
  3. Answers may vary.
  4. Choose: I speak English.
Teacher / Academic Note

This chapter addresses subject omission, a common area where Spanish-speaking learners may transfer patterns from Spanish into English. In second language learning, this kind of predictable transfer can be reduced through noticing, contrastive examples, repeated input, and deliberate practice (Swan, 2016; Swan & Smith, 2001).

Quick Review
  • Learn the English pattern as a whole structure.
  • Do not translate word-for-word from Spanish.
  • Practice with short, correct sentences before building longer ones.
  • Use the examples in this chapter as sentence models.
Sources and Further Reading
  • Swan, 2016; Swan & Smith, 2001
